name: Sibutramine

lead: Sibutramine was a prescription weight-loss pill that made people feel full sooner. Cutting forum users saw it as a substitute for or complement to an ECA stack, aimed at lower body fat through eating less.

It blocks reuptake of serotonin and norepinephrine in the brain, increasing fullness and reducing food intake. Randomised trials found it produced modest weight loss beyond diet and exercise. In 2010 the SCOUT outcomes trial in more than 10,000 overweight or obese people with cardiovascular disease or diabetes found more heart attacks and strokes, and regulators suspended or withdrew it.

paras: It was sold as Meridia (US) and Reductil (elsewhere) and has only scattered mentions on bodybuilding forums such as T Nation, where users compared it with ECA stacks before and after withdrawal. It is also known as an undeclared ingredient in some weight-loss supplements.

Reported effects include raised heart rate and blood pressure, dry mouth, insomnia and constipation, and a case report of psychosis. Regulators withdrew it in the EU and US in 2010 over cardiovascular risk.

What the Hell is Wrong with Me?

angle.text: Sibutramine is a withdrawn appetite suppressant that cutting forum users saw as a substitute or complement to an ECA stack. It blocks serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake so you feel full sooner and eat less. Randomised trials found modest weight loss beyond diet and exercise.

lead: Sibutramine, sold as Meridia in the United States and Reductil elsewhere, is an appetite suppressant that was prescribed for obesity from the late 1990s until it was withdrawn from major markets in 2010 [1][2][3]. It works by making people feel full sooner, so they eat less; in the physique and fitness world the appeal was the same chain every dieting aid is used for: lower calorie intake, more fat lost, a leaner and more defined look [1][4][5].

Randomised placebo-controlled trials found dose-related weight loss in the 1990s, and the two-year STORM trial examined weight maintenance on the drug [6][7]. In 2010 the SCOUT outcomes trial, which followed nearly ten thousand older adults with cardiovascular disease or type 2 diabetes, found more non-fatal heart attacks and strokes on sibutramine than on placebo, and regulators in Europe and the US moved to suspend or withdraw it [8][9][3].

In bodybuilding and fitness forums such as T Nation, members compared sibutramine with ECA stacks, phentermine and other appetite suppressants, before and after withdrawal [4][5]. It also became known as an undeclared ingredient in products sold as herbal or natural weight-loss supplements, which the FDA has warned about repeatedly since 2008 [3].

paras: Sibutramine was approved by the FDA in November 1997 for adults with a BMI of 30 or higher, or 27 or higher with comorbid conditions, in addition to diet and exercise [1]. An obesity-guideline from endocrinologists and a systematic review of emerging obesity drugs place it among historical pharmacotherapies [10][11]. A US trial registry lists a study in binge-eating disorder and trials in adolescents [12][13].

Randomised placebo-controlled trials in the 1990s found dose-related weight loss [6][14]. A general reference reports about 4.5 kg greater loss than placebo at one year in meta-analytic data [1]. The STORM study followed participants for two years after initial weight loss and compared continued treatment with placebo [7]. Reviews of weight-loss trials with at least one year of follow-up and a meta-analysis of long-term pharmacotherapy included sibutramine [15][16].

Commonly reported effects include dry mouth, insomnia, constipation, headache, nausea, dizziness and raised heart rate and blood pressure; paradoxically increased appetite is also listed [1][3]. Less common effects include arrhythmias and mental changes such as confusion or depression, and a case report described a psychotic episode associated with sibutramine [3].

SCOUT enrolled 10,744 adults aged 55 or older with cardiovascular disease, type 2 diabetes or both; after a six-week single-blind lead-in, 9,804 were randomised and followed for a mean of 3.4 years [8]. The primary composite (non-fatal heart attack, non-fatal stroke, resuscitated cardiac arrest or cardiovascular death) occurred in 11.4 percent on sibutramine versus 10.0 percent on placebo (hazard ratio 1.16) [8]. Non-fatal heart attack (4.1 vs 3.2 percent) and non-fatal stroke (2.6 vs 1.9 percent) were higher; cardiovascular death and all-cause death were not [8].

Sibutramine inhibits reuptake of serotonin and norepinephrine, with a weaker effect on dopamine, which increases satiety [1]. Wikipedia reports that in humans it reduces reuptake of norepinephrine by roughly 73 percent, serotonin by 54 percent and dopamine by 16 percent [3].

It acts largely as a prodrug: its desmethyl metabolites (M1 and M2) are much more potent than the parent compound, and the (R)-enantiomers have stronger appetite-suppressing effects [3]. Oral absorption is about 77 percent with considerable first-pass metabolism, mainly through CYP3A4, about 97 percent protein binding and mostly urinary excretion; the parent half-life is about one hour and the metabolites about 14 and 16 hours [1][3]. Studies have also examined its effect on norepinephrine transporter activity in tilt-induced presyncope [17].

Boots Pharmaceuticals in Nottingham developed sibutramine (BTS 54524) in 1988, originally as an antidepressant candidate; animal studies showing reduced food intake redirected it toward obesity [1][3]. After BASF/Knoll AG bought Boots' research division in 1995, Knoll marketed it, and Abbott Laboratories later manufactured and sold it in the US [3]. The FDA approved Meridia in November 1997 for people with a BMI of 30 or more, or 27 or more with cardiovascular risk factors, and it was scheduled as a Schedule IV drug [3].
The SCOUT trial ran from January 2003 to November 2005 and was published in the New England Journal of Medicine in September 2010 [8][3].

Wikipedia records that the advocacy group Public Citizen petitioned the FDA to ban sibutramine in 2002, that the FDA did not withdraw it then, and that FDA staff scientist David Graham testified to a US Senate committee in November 2004 about concerns over the agency's handling of drug safety [3]. After SCOUT, the European Medicines Agency recommended suspending marketing authorisations on 21 January 2010; in August 2010 the FDA added a contraindication for patients over 65; and on 8 October 2010 the FDA recommended against continued use and Abbott withdrew the drug from the US market [3]. The Medical Letter reported the withdrawal the same year [2]. It was subsequently withdrawn in many other countries, including Australia, Canada, China, India, New Zealand, Thailand and the UK [3].

Not everyone read the trial the same way. In April 2010 David Haslam of the UK's National Obesity Forum argued that SCOUT enrolled only high-cardiovascular-risk patients and therefore did not reflect typical people with obesity, according to Wikipedia [3]. SCOUT's authors reported that the increase was in non-fatal heart attack and stroke, not in cardiovascular or all-cause death [8]. Wikipedia lists the main controversies as the speed of regulators' response to early safety signals and the question of how far the SCOUT population generalises [3].

According to Wikipedia, contraindications included eating disorders, severe depression, mania, a history of substance abuse, age under 18 or over 65, uncontrolled hypertension, cardiovascular disease, epilepsy and closed-angle glaucoma [3]. Combination with MAO inhibitors carried a risk of serotonin syndrome, and CYP3A4 inhibitors such as ketoconazole and erythromycin could raise sibutramine levels; a 2016 Cochrane review is cited as finding substantial rises in blood pressure and heart rate in some patients [3].

The FDA alerted consumers in December 2008 to 27 products sold as dietary supplements that contained undisclosed sibutramine, recalled 34 more in April 2009, and in October 2011 warned about 20 tainted brands, according to Wikipedia [3]. In December 2010 the FDA said that all versions of one product, Fruta Planta, contained it, and a January 2010 case involved counterfeit Alli sold online that contained sibutramine rather than orlistat [3]. Health Canada and the UK's MHRA issued similar warnings in 2010, and a 2018 FDA study found synthetic additives including sibutramine in more than 700 products marketed as natural or herbal [3].

subs.h: Use in looksmaxxing and fitness communities
paras: T Nation threads have discussed sibutramine alongside ECA stacks, phentermine and other appetite suppressants; one 2009 thread asked about Meridia versus an ECA stack after a doctor suggested it [4][5]. One forum user listed it among pharmaceutical options for combined appetite suppression and said side effects were a consideration [5]. A 2010 T Nation thread on government regulation of supplements also touched on it [18].

Human studies are extensive. SCOUT, a randomised trial of 10,744 high-risk participants, assessed cardiovascular outcomes [8]. STORM examined weight maintenance after weight loss in a two-year randomised design [7]. Earlier randomised trials found dose-related weight loss [6][14]. Meta-analyses of obesity drugs also include it [15][16][19]. Registered trials examined sibutramine in adolescents, in binge-eating disorder, and with metformin [12][13][20].

lore.intro: In bodybuilding forums sibutramine is mentioned as a former prescription appetite suppressant, discussed beside ECA stacks and other stimulants for cutting phases [4][5]. Most later discussion concerns its presence in adulterated supplements and its withdrawal.

claims.claim: Sibutramine is a strong appetite suppressant that can substitute for or complement an ECA stack.
Combining appetite suppressants and other agents improves fat loss.
The SCOUT result applies only to high-risk patients, not to healthy dieters.
Products labelled herbal or natural for weight loss contain only plant ingredients.
Sibutramine remains safe to use outside medical supervision.
